**LITTLE ROCK, Arkansas (CNN) —** As Carlotta Walls LaNier flips through her high school yearbook, she points out the only two African Americans in her senior class. She pauses at a photograph on a page dedicated to “Integration.”

Nearly five decades have passed since LaNier graduated from Little Rock Central High School in Arkansas. “It shows how the 101st were on the grounds of the school,” she says.

In 1957, soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division, an elite Army unit, escorted LaNier and eight other African-American students into the all-white public high school. The students, who became known as the Little Rock Nine, were taunted and threatened by an angry mob.

“We knew we could not participate in extracurricular activities,” LaNier recalls. “There was one who could have been in the band, one who could have been on track. I was the one who played basketball. … I couldn’t do that.”

At the time, LaNier believed that once the doors to equality had opened, it would not be long before an African American became president.

“I had hoped to see something like that in the next 10 or 15 years when I was in high school, but that didn’t happen,” she says.

What has happened, however, is that a new generation of students now walks the halls of Central High. Although the school’s exterior looks much as it did during integration, the interior would be almost unrecognizable to LaNier and the other members of the Little Rock Nine.

“I can’t believe it happened here, but I’m glad it did,” one student says.

Today, the sea of mostly white faces has disappeared, and the hallways are filled with a more racially diverse student body. Students take a class about the school’s history, and many say it has given them a greater appreciation for racial tolerance.

“Now it’s definitely hard to imagine—you walk into the halls and you see people of all different races in the hallway. And, in addition, the majority of our school is African American now,” says student body president Afshar Sanati. “It is hard for me to walk inside the school every day and see how this place could have been such a hostile environment for nine African-American students.”

LaNier remains humble when reflecting on her experience.

“We all knew that we were giving up something for a bigger cause, and [we were] happy that we did it,” she says. “Because it has been 51 years, I think they were baby steps now. But they were big steps then.”

The steps taken by the Little Rock Nine were so significant that LaNier and the other eight members received personal invitations to attend President-elect Barack Obama’s inauguration.

“I think the Little Rock Nine set the foundation,” says student Sarah Karney. “I don’t think [Obama’s election] could have happened without them.”

Today, many students at Central High see themselves as beneficiaries of an Obama presidency.

“Him being president means there actually is a chance for anyone to do what they want to do if they work hard enough,” says Helena Liu, who adds that she does not see race when she looks at Obama.

“It doesn’t depend on your race—it depends on who you are, the quality of your character,” says DeIvory Howard.

“[We’ve] got to get past just the color of our skins being newsworthy. It’s really about all the things we knew we could do for this country, and now we have the opportunity to show it, and it’s going to come through his leadership,” LaNier says. “And we’re looking forward to that.”

Senior Chris Bell could not agree more.

“This election proves that this America is just not the old America. It shows that America is ready for something different,” Bell says. “I just think … that’s amazing.”

The nine students—later called the Little Rock Nine—faced threats and insults from a furious crowd.

As a high school student, she believed opening the way toward equality would soon lead to the election of a Black president. She had hoped it would happen within 10 or 15 years, but it took much longer.

In the meantime, a different generation has taken LaNier’s place in Central High’s corridors. Although the building’s outside appearance remains much as it was during desegregation, its interior and student population would seem almost unfamiliar to the Little Rock Nine.

One student expressed disbelief that such events occurred at the school while also saying they were glad integration happened there. The overwhelmingly white student body of the past is gone, replaced by students from a far broader range of racial backgrounds. Pupils now study the school’s history in class, and many say those lessons have deepened their respect for racial tolerance.

Student body president Afshar Sanati says it is difficult to picture the former reality because students of many races now share the hallways, and African-Americans make up most of the school’s enrollment. He finds it especially hard to imagine that the building he enters each day was once so dangerous and unwelcoming for nine Black students.

Looking back, LaNier remains modest about her role. She says all nine understood they were making personal sacrifices in service of something larger and were pleased to do so. After 51 years, their actions may appear to her like small, early advances, but at the time they represented enormous progress.

The Little Rock Nine’s contribution was significant enough that all nine received individual invitations to the inauguration of President-elect Barack Obama. Central High student Sarah Karney believes they helped lay the groundwork for his election and doubts it could have occurred without what they did.

Many current students view themselves as people who will benefit from an Obama administration. Helena Liu says his presidency demonstrates that anyone can pursue an ambition through sufficient effort. When she looks at Obama, she says, race is not what she notices.

DeIvory Howard similarly argues that achievement is determined not by race but by a person’s identity and strength of character.

LaNier says society must move beyond treating skin color alone as something newsworthy. In her view, African-Americans have long known what they could contribute to the United States, and Obama’s leadership now offers an opportunity to demonstrate it. She says she looks forward to seeing that happen.

Senior Chris Bell shares that enthusiasm. For him, the election shows that today’s United States is no longer the country it once was and is prepared to embrace change—something he considers remarkable.

She was 14 years old, the youngest of the Little Rock Nine — the group of Black students who integrated the Arkansas school in 1957 after the US Supreme Court ruled segregated public schools unconstitutional.

The students encountered angry crowds, threats and daily harassment. Arkansas Gov. Orval Faubus initially deployed the National Guard to prevent them from entering the school. President Dwight D. Eisenhower later federalized the Guard and sent members of the Army’s 101st Airborne Division to enforce the court order.

For LaNier, the experience was not framed as an attempt to become a civil rights icon. She wanted access to the same educational opportunities available to White students and believed attending Central High would help secure her future.

That decision placed her at the center of a national confrontation over race, education and the authority of the federal government.

LaNier remained at Central despite intimidation and violence, graduating in 1960. She became the first Black girl to receive a diploma from the school.

Decades later, she was invited to Washington for Obama’s inauguration on January 20, 2009 — an event that carried deep personal meaning for someone who had once needed soldiers to enter a public school.

From the inauguration, LaNier could look back on a span of history that connected the struggle to desegregate a Southern high school with the election of a Black president. The moment, she has said in reflections on her life, demonstrated how far the country had moved since 1957.

But it did not erase the past or signal that the work was complete.

Schools across the United States remain divided along racial and economic lines, often because of housing patterns, district boundaries and unequal access to resources. LaNier has continued to speak to students and educators about the Little Rock Nine, emphasizing that civil rights gains must be protected and expanded by each generation.

In 1999, LaNier and the other members of the Little Rock Nine received the Congressional Gold Medal, one of the nation’s highest civilian honors.

Her journey from Central High to a presidential inauguration reflects both the scale of America’s progress and the persistence required to achieve it. What began with nine teenagers walking past a hostile crowd became part of a broader movement that reshaped the country.

Obama’s inauguration offered a powerful symbol of that change. For LaNier, however, the lesson of Little Rock remains grounded not only in historic milestones, but also in the choices of ordinary people willing to insist that constitutional rights apply to everyone.

## From Central High to the White House

On a September morning in 1957, 14-year-old Carlotta Walls LaNier walked toward Little Rock Central High School through a crowd determined to keep her out.

Federal troops from the 101st Airborne Division escorted her and eight other Black students past jeering segregationists and into the imposing school. Their enrollment, ordered after the Supreme Court outlawed school segregation, became one of the defining confrontations of the civil-rights era.

Fifty-one years later, LaNier watched Americans elect Barack Obama as the nation’s first Black president.

The distance between those moments can be measured in years, laws and elections. For LaNier, the youngest of the Little Rock Nine, it could also be measured personally: from needing soldiers to enter a public school to seeing a Black family prepare to enter the White House.

LaNier greeted Obama’s 2008 victory with pride and a sense of vindication. In public reflections surrounding the election, she described it as evidence of how far the country had traveled since the days when her presence in a classroom provoked a constitutional crisis. The sacrifices made in Little Rock, she said, helped widen opportunities not only for Black students but for generations of Americans.

Yet she resisted treating the election as the end of that struggle. Obama’s victory was a milestone, not proof that racial inequality had disappeared. The lesson of Central High, LaNier has repeatedly emphasized, is that progress depends on people who are willing to claim their rights—and on institutions willing to defend them.

The connection was especially vivid inside Central High itself. The school that once symbolized massive resistance to integration had become a diverse campus and a National Historic Site. Students walked past photographs of the Little Rock Nine and attended classes in halls where federal soldiers once stood guard.

After Obama’s election, students described a mixture of excitement, disbelief and historical awareness. For Black students, seeing a person who looked like them win the presidency expanded their sense of what was possible. Others saw the result as evidence that young people and voters across racial lines could reshape the country. But students also noted that racial divisions remained visible in schools, neighborhoods and politics.

That tension—between celebration and unfinished work—links 1957 and 2008.

The Little Rock Nine did not know exactly where their walk would lead. Their immediate goal was more basic: to receive the education the Constitution promised them. They endured insults, isolation and threats. One member, Minnijean Brown, was expelled after responding to repeated harassment. Ernest Green became Central High’s first Black graduate in 1958, receiving his diploma as the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. watched.

Obama’s election grew from the broader movement to which their courage belonged. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 dismantled legal segregation. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 attacked barriers designed to keep Black citizens from the polls. Decades of organizing turned rights written on paper into political power.

None of that made Obama’s victory inevitable. But it made it possible.

At Central High, history is not confined to a textbook. It is embedded in the building’s stone façade, in the memorials across the street and in the students who continue to pass through its doors. For them, Obama’s election offered a new chapter in a story their school helped write.

LaNier’s journey captures the scale of the change. In 1957, government power had to be used to protect a Black child seeking a desk in a public classroom. In 2008, voters used their own power to send a Black man to the nation’s highest office.

Between those two images lies more than half a century of struggle. And in the reactions of LaNier and Central High’s students was a shared understanding: history can move, but only when people push it forward.

At 14 years old, Carlotta Walls LaNier walked into Little Rock Central High School as one of nine Black students challenging segregation in Arkansas public schools.

**[VIDEO: LaNier turning the pages of a yearbook]**

**REPORTER (V.O.):**  
Decades later, LaNier opens a yearbook filled with familiar faces—and painful memories.

**CARLOTTA WALLS LANIER:**  
You look at these pictures and see teenagers at school activities, smiling and enjoying themselves. But that was not the experience we had. We were there to get an education, and every day required courage and determination.

**REPORTER:**  
A chapter of American history preserved on these pages, and a lesson LaNier says remains urgently relevant today.

# From Central High to the Capitol: The Little Rock Nine Witness Obama’s Inauguration

*Editor’s note: The historical quotations below come from public speeches and archival records. Because no original interviews were provided, comments from present-day Central High students are clearly marked as reporting placeholders rather than fabricated quotations.*

WASHINGTON — More than half a century after nine Black teenagers walked through the doors of Little Rock Central High School under military protection, members of the Little Rock Nine traveled to Washington to watch Barack Obama take the oath of office as the nation’s first Black president.

On Jan. 20, 2009, they joined a crowd stretching from the U.S. Capitol toward the Lincoln Memorial—a landscape already heavy with the history of the civil rights movement. For the former students who had challenged segregation in 1957, Obama’s inauguration represented both an extraordinary milestone and a reminder of the struggle that made it possible.

During the ceremony, Obama acknowledged that long history without suggesting it had ended.

“This is the meaning of our liberty and our creed,” he said in his inaugural address, describing a nation in which people of different races and faiths could gather to celebrate the peaceful transfer of power. “On this day, we gather because we have chosen hope over fear, unity of purpose over conflict and discord.”

For the Little Rock Nine, the scene stood in stark contrast to the one they had encountered at Central High.

## The crisis at Central High

In its 1954 decision in *Brown v. Board of Education*, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that state-mandated segregation in public schools was unconstitutional. But implementation met determined resistance across the South.

Three years later, Arkansas Gov. Orval Faubus ordered the Arkansas National Guard to prevent nine Black students from entering Central High. The students—Melba Pattillo Beals, Minnijean Brown Trickey, Elizabeth Eckford, Ernest Green, Gloria Ray Karlmark, Carlotta Walls LaNier, Terrence Roberts, Jefferson Thomas and Thelma Mothershed Wair—faced crowds that shouted threats and racial slurs.

Eckford, then 15, became the subject of one of the most enduring photographs of the civil rights era. Wearing sunglasses and carrying her books, she walked alone toward a bus stop while a white mob followed her.

The confrontation became a test of federal authority. On Sept. 24, 1957, President Dwight D. Eisenhower addressed the nation and announced that he was sending federal troops to Little Rock.

“Mob rule cannot be allowed to override the decisions of our courts,” Eisenhower said.

Soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division escorted the nine students into Central High the following day. Federal protection, however, did not shield them from all the abuse inside the school. They endured harassment, isolation and physical attacks throughout the academic year.

In May 1958, Ernest Green became the first Black student to graduate from Central High. Martin Luther King Jr. attended the ceremony.

## A journey measured in generations

By the time Obama was inaugurated, the Little Rock Nine had spent decades speaking about education, equality and the unfinished work of civil rights. Congress awarded the group its highest civilian honor, the Congressional Gold Medal, in 1999.

Their presence at the 2009 inauguration created a direct link between two defining moments in American history: the federal enforcement of school desegregation and the election of a Black president.

The connection was not evidence that the country had moved cleanly beyond racism. Rather, it showed how protest, court rulings, federal action and the courage of young people could widen the boundaries of American democracy.

Obama made a similar point in his address, placing his election within a history of sacrifice.

“This is the journey we continue today,” he said. “We remain the most prosperous, powerful nation on Earth. Our workers are no less productive than when this crisis began. Our minds are no less inventive, our goods and services no less needed than they were last week or last month or last year.”

The Little Rock Nine knew more than most that progress did not arrive automatically. In 1957, they had not entered Central High as national monuments. They had entered as teenagers expected to attend class while adults fought over their right to be there.

In 2009, they watched another barrier fall.

## The history students inherit

Today, Central High remains an operating public school as well as a National Historic Site. Its students attend classes in a building recognized around the world, passing through the same entrance that became a battleground over equal education.

That history can feel both immediate and difficult to comprehend.

Some students encounter the Little Rock Nine first in elementary-school lessons or museum exhibits. At Central, however, the story becomes part of daily life—visible in the school’s architecture, its memorials and the visitors who arrive to stand across the street and imagine the events of 1957.

The inauguration may now seem distant to students who were born after 2009. Yet its relationship to Central High remains relevant. Obama’s election did not erase disparities in school funding, academic opportunity or discipline. Nor did it settle national disputes over how racism should be taught.

Those student voices are essential because the legacy of the Little Rock Nine does not belong only to textbooks or anniversary ceremonies. It is inherited by each new class entering Central High.

## A milestone, not an ending

The distance between Little Rock in 1957 and Washington in 2009 can be measured in years, but also in choices: nine students choosing to return to school despite danger; families choosing to stand behind them; lawyers continuing to press constitutional claims; and federal officials eventually choosing to enforce the law.

Obama’s inauguration embodied the results of those choices. It also underscored the distinction between a breakthrough and a conclusion.

The Little Rock Nine helped open doors they had every reason to fear walking through. Decades later, they stood at the Capitol as a Black president took an oath that, in 1957, many Americans could scarcely have imagined.

Their journey from Central High to the inauguration did not mean the nation had completed its work. It meant that work could produce change—and that another generation would be responsible for deciding what came next.
